triage.name: Chalazion
triage.reason: Painless eyelid nodule distinguished from hordeolum by history and exam; a straightforward but instructive eyelid lesion case.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'Biopsy of eyelid lesion' was in confirmatory, not_indicated; kept confirmatory as a conditional order (only if lesion is recurrent, ulcerated, has loss of eyelashes, or fails to resolve with conservative treatment)

demographics: Most common in adults, but occurs in children and older adults

chief_complaints.text: I have a bump on my eyelid

hpi.duration: Usually present for weeks to months before medical evaluation
hpi.progression: Begins as a small, painless nodule within the eyelid; it may slowly enlarge and occasionally become red and tender if secondarily inflamed or infected
hpi.location: Upper or lower eyelid, most often the upper; within the tarsal plate, sometimes visible on the inner surface of the eyelid
hpi.quality: Firm, round, non-tender or mildly tender nodule; may feel like a pea under the skin
hpi.severity: Mild; usually painless, but can cause a sense of heaviness or pressure
hpi.timing: Constant; does not vary with time of day

associated_symptoms.text: Blurred vision from pressure on the eye

atypical.how_it_differs: Chalazia may be noticed only by parents as a painless lid lump; recurrent lesions are often associated with blepharokeratoconjunctivitis and may be mislabeled as styes.
A persistent or recurrent single nodule should raise concern for sebaceous gland carcinoma; look for loss of eyelashes, ulceration, or bleeding.
Secondary bacterial infection can develop more rapidly, presenting as acute tender swelling that may mimic preseptal cellulitis.

general.mild: Well-appearing; small palpable nodule in the eyelid, often found incidentally
general.moderate: Comfortable; visible eyelid nodule with mild localized swelling, no systemic signs
general.severe: Large nodule deforming the eyelid contour or partially obstructing the pupil; may have mild erythema and tenderness, but no fever
general.critical: Secondary preseptal cellulitis with red, warm, swollen eyelid; patient may have low-grade fever but remains alert, without proptosis or pain with eye movement

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently palpate the eyelid, and evert the lid to view the conjunctival surface
findings.finding: Firm, round, non-tender nodule within the eyelid, often visible under the skin or as a yellow-white nodule on the tarsal conjunctiva
Mild tenderness of the eyelid around the nodule, more pronounced if secondarily inflamed
Erythema of overlying eyelid skin, especially if inflamed

findings.maneuver: Inspect lid margin and conjunctiva, press on lacrimal sac
Inspect the eyelid margin and lashes
findings.finding: No loss of eyelashes, ulceration, or bleeding

findings.maneuver: Assess eye position from above and from the side

findings.text: Well-defined, hypoechoic nodule within the tarsal plate

confirmatory.why: Confirms the diagnosis when a recurrent or atypical lesion raises concern for sebaceous cell carcinoma or other malignancy.
confirmatory.only_if: lesion is recurrent, ulcerated, has loss of eyelashes, or fails to resolve with conservative treatment

not_indicated.why: No systemic signs; chalazion is a localized eyelid process.
Inflammatory markers do not change management in a typical chalazion.
Not indicated for clinical diagnosis of a typical chalazion.

decision_points: Consider biopsy if the lesion is recurrent, ulcerated, associated with loss of eyelashes, or fails to resolve after weeks of conservative therapy.

differential.name: Hordeolum (stye)
differential.why_considered: Acute painful eyelid lump near the lid margin; students may confuse it with chalazion because both involve eyelid glands.

history: Painful and tender from the start
May point at the lid margin and drain pus
exam: Tender, erythematous papule or pustule at the lid margin
Localized lid margin swelling rather than a deeper tarsal nodule
May have pointing or discharge

differential.name: Preseptal cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Eyelid erythema, warmth, and swelling can accompany an inflamed chalazion or secondary infection.
differential.trigger: Rapidly spreading eyelid redness and swelling, fever, or a skin break on the eyelid

history: Rapid progression over hours to a day
Recent trauma, insect bite, or sinus infection
exam: Warm, tender, diffusely swollen eyelid without a discrete nodule
Erythema extending beyond the nodule
No proptosis and full painless eye movements
labs: May have leukocytosis if systemic involvement
imaging: CT orbit may show preseptal soft tissue swelling and no postseptal involvement if diagnosis unclear

differential.name: Sebaceous gland carcinoma
differential.why_considered: Can present as a painless, firm eyelid nodule and is the classic malignancy mistaken for chalazion.
differential.trigger: Recurrent or persistent solitary eyelid nodule in an older adult, especially with loss of eyelashes or ulceration

history: Recurrent nodule in the same location after treatment
exam: Loss of eyelashes
Ulceration or bleeding
Yellowish appearance of the conjunctiva or nodule
Fixation to tarsus or lid margin
labs: Biopsy shows sebaceous carcinoma with pagetoid spread
imaging: Full-thickness eyelid biopsy rather than imaging for diagnosis

differential.name: Basal cell carcinoma
differential.why_considered: Firm, painless eyelid nodule; most common eyelid malignancy.
differential.trigger: Painless nodule with rolled pearly border, telangiectasias, or ulceration, especially lower eyelid

history: Long-standing lesion that does not resolve
exam: Pearly, waxy nodule with telangiectasias
Rolled, raised border
Ulceration with crusting
Usually lower eyelid

differential.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
differential.why_considered: Eyelid nodule or plaque that can resemble chalazion, but usually scaly or ulcerated.

exam: Scaly, crusted, or ulcerated plaque or nodule
May be firm with irregular border
No discrete tarsal nodule

differential.name: Dermoid cyst
differential.why_considered: Smooth, firm, painless eyelid or periocular mass, especially in children or young adults.

exam: Smooth, round, mobile mass often superotemporal
No overlying skin change
No loss of eyelashes
imaging: Ultrasound or CT shows cystic lesion with fat or calcification if needed

differential.name: Pyogenic granuloma
differential.why_considered: Red, raised eyelid lesion that may appear after trauma, surgery, or a chronic chalazion.

history: Recent lid surgery, trauma, or prior chalazion
exam: Friable, red, pedunculated papule
Moist surface, often bleeding or crusted

differential.name: Molluscum contagiosum
differential.why_considered: Small eyelid margin or periocular papule, can cause mechanical conjunctivitis.

history: Multiple small lesions on face or body
exam: Dome-shaped, waxy papule with central umbilication
May be single or multiple at lid margin

severity.mild: Small, painless eyelid nodule, often less than a few millimeters, with no overlying skin change and no effect on vision.
severity.moderate: Larger nodule causing visible lid fullness or mild pressure, with occasional mild tenderness or redness but no visual symptoms.
severity.severe: Large or recurrent nodule producing eyelid deformity, corneal pressure with blurred or distorted vision, secondary inflammation, or failure to resolve after weeks of conservative care.

red_flags.finding: Recurrent or persistent nodule in the same location, especially with loss of eyelashes, ulceration, or bleeding
red_flags.meaning: Possible sebaceous gland carcinoma; biopsy is needed

red_flags.finding: Fever with rapidly spreading eyelid redness and warmth
red_flags.meaning: Secondary preseptal cellulitis; may need systemic antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Proptosis, painful eye movements, or decreased vision
red_flags.meaning: Possible orbital cellulitis or orbital extension; emergency

red_flags.finding: Blurred or distorted vision from a large upper lid lesion
red_flags.meaning: Corneal compression or astigmatism; needs prompt ophthalmic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Acute painful, tender, red bump at the lid margin
red_flags.meaning: More consistent with hordeolum; not a typical chalazion

complications.name: Spontaneous drainage
clues: Discharge of oily or purulent material

complications.name: Recurrence
clues: Underlying blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction

special_populations.differences: Recurrent chalazia often occur with blepharokeratoconjunctivitis; large upper lid lesions can induce astigmatism and amblyopia, so vision must be checked.
A solitary, recurrent, or non-resolving nodule is concerning for sebaceous gland carcinoma; biopsy earlier.
Secondary bacterial infection may develop more quickly and present as preseptal cellulitis rather than a quiet nodule.
May be more prone to recurrent chalazia and secondary infection; underlying blood glucose control should be reviewed.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the bump, and how has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months; slow or stable growth, not rapid enlargement

key_questions.question: Is the bump painful or tender?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent or minimal pain; prominent pain suggests an inflamed chalazion, hordeolum, or secondary infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any blurred, distorted, or double vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Normal vision; any visual change suggests corneal pressure from a large upper lid lesion or orbital involvement

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any loss of eyelashes, ulceration, bleeding, or crusting on the bump?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these features raise concern for sebaceous cell carcinoma

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, rapidly spreading redness, or a hot, swollen eyelid?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these suggest preseptal cellulitis rather than uncomplicated chalazion

key_questions.question: Have you had a bump like this before, or do you have blepharitis, rosacea, or seborrheic dermatitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent lesions or underlying eyelid disease, which predisposes to chalazion

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes or any condition that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes or immunocompromise, which may increase risk and recurrence

key_questions.question: Do you wear contact lenses, use eye makeup, or frequently rub your eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Contributing habits to address during treatment

reasoning_points: Painless, gradually enlarging eyelid nodule over weeks to months
Firm, round, non-tender nodule within the tarsal plate on exam
No acute inflammatory signs such as marked erythema, warmth, or purulent discharge
No visual changes or ocular symptoms
No loss of eyelashes, ulceration, or bleeding
Underlying risk factors such as blepharitis, rosacea, or seborrheic dermatitis support the diagnosis
Diagnosis is clinical; biopsy is reserved for recurrent or atypical lesions

easy: Adult with a painless upper eyelid bump for weeks
No visual changes, no lash loss
Classic firm, mobile tarsal nodule on exam
medium: Inflamed chalazion with overlying erythema and tenderness mimicking hordeolum
Recurrent chalazion in a patient with blepharitis or rosacea
Child with a large upper lid chalazion and concern for astigmatism
Contact lens wearer with eyelid irritation and fluctuating nodule
hard: Older adult with a solitary, recurrent, non-resolving nodule raising concern for sebaceous gland carcinoma
Secondary preseptal cellulitis with fever and spreading eyelid redness
Large upper lid chalazion causing blurred or distorted vision and requiring ophthalmic evaluation
Atypical lesion with lash loss or ulceration requiring biopsy
